heroHeadline: Haiti Presses UN to Renew Gang Suppression Force Mandate as Self-Defense Brigades Complicate Security Handover
heroSubtitle: In the aftermath of the August 23 Kenscoff church massacre that killed at least 47 people, hundreds of mourners gathered August 30 for the first funeral service — laying to rest four victims, including a mother, father and son — while armed civilians stood guard outside amid fears of another raid. Per the joint PNH/AFH/GSF plan agreed after the massacre, the Gang Suppression Force began taking over PNH security positions in Kenscoff on September 1, then launched a new operational phase of joint patrols with police in downtown Port-au-Prince on September 3, as national police redeployed to reinforce Kenscoff. A collective funeral for 20+ more victims drew hundreds on September 2, with only 17 of 47 buried by that point and survivors still describing the community as on "red alert." On September 4, Haiti's Foreign Ministry formally asked the UN Security Council to renew the GSF's mandate — set to expire September 30, 2026 absent Council action — with Foreign Minister Raina Forbin saying Haiti needs "technical, financial, logistical and safety support that is up to the challenge" and OAS Secretary-General Albert Ramdin calling the country's situation a "critical juncture." A September 7 Washington Post feature and ACLED analysis further detailed how armed self-defense brigades in Artibonite, like the Coalition des Révolutionnaires pour Sauver l'Artibonite, have evolved from community protectors into militias implicated in mass killings and civilian abuse, complicating the GSF's push to consolidate a legitimate, accountable security response as its roughly 1,000 deployed personnel remain well short of the 5,550-person authorized ceiling.
